Completely re-write the lightmap generation code:
- Follow the general lightmapper code structure from 4.0.
- Use proper path tracing to compute the global illumination.
- Use atlassing to merge all lightmaps into a single texture (done by @RandomShaper)
- Use OpenImageDenoiser to improve the generated lightmaps.

There is some minor compatibility breakage in some properties and methods
in BakedLightmap, but lightmaps generated in previous engine versions
should work fine out of the box.

The scene importer has been changed to generate `.unwrap_cache` files
next to the imported scene files. These files *SHOULD* be added to any
version control system as they guarantee there won't be differences when
re-importing the scene from other OSes or engine versions.

Documentation is missing, I'll work on it after the holidays :)

This work started as a Google Summer of Code project; Was later funded by IMVU for a good amount of progress;
Was then finished and polished by me on my free time.

TPS demo with direct light only:
![lm-off](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4402304/103029621-79eed300-455a-11eb-8eea-fc14e52c79be.png)

TPS demo with baked indirect lighting.
![lm-on](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4402304/103029614-778c7900-455a-11eb-85dc-b54b6a8e3974.png)

Special thanks to Pedro (@RandomShaper) for helping out with atlassing and other issues!

Supersedes #40035.
This closes #15055, closes #16820, closes #16398, closes #20321, closes #21587, closes #30789, closes #30929, closes #32746, closes #38685, closes #39532.

Edit:
I updated the PR with fixes for all the issues reported so far:
* Fix Embree runtime when using MinGW (patch by @RandomShaper), closes #45097.
* Fix baking of lightmaps on GridMaps, closes #45086.
* Fix some GLSL errors, should fix #45091 but I don't have a proper way to test it on a mac.
* Fix overflow in the number of shader variants (GLES2), it made gizmos go black. Reported via twitter, no issue open AFAIK.

@esblinuxcss this is expected, the cone tracing mode of the previous light mapper was a fast but inaccurate mode based off of GiProbe. The new lightmapper uses a much better version of the raytrace mode of the previous lightmapper. In addition you are using 15 bounces the previous lightmapper only used 1, more bounces more time. Also Highquality mode takes more time,you should be able to get an acceptable result with low. Try it on low with 3 bounces. 

Make sure you are building with target=release_debug or you are downloading an artifact from here which is compiled using release_debug.

@esblinuxcss We could consider adding an easy way to bake with a "preview" quality before committing to a "final" bake. This way, you could keep your current settings in your BakedLightmap node, yet you'd have the ability to perform a quick bake with low quality settings.

I opened a proposal to discuss this: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2029

Sorry I wasn't able to spend a lot of time looking, I've mainly just looked at the functionality of this version. I've only looked at the lightmap generation and not the use in a game situation. Overall it seems quite polished, and the user interface is nice and it tends to produce usable results. :+1: :smile: 

Just to point out a few nitpicks:
* Lights don't seem to have volume, so you don't get soft shadows (at least in the first pass). This is one of the major advantages of baked light so it would be nice to get this in the next version. You can get soft light by using emission or sky however.

You can also see aliasing which occurs with thin geometry, this can be also dealt with by volumetric lights. Look at the shadows cast by the railings:
![lightmap_aliasing](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/21999379/103345092-565ee780-4a88-11eb-9406-11605d26ac58.png)

* Skies - In general I think this is problematic in godot, not just in lightmap but in the PBR. The problem is getting a blue hue from blue skies. This is a standard sky (boosted a bit because it is seems overly hard to get it light enough to appear on the lightmap):

![lightmap_sunandsky](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/21999379/103345296-f0bf2b00-4a88-11eb-9bef-81b2af9d5678.png)

This is understandable because most of the samples are hitting blue sky in the procedural sky.

This is turning down the blue energy to zero and turning up the sun itself (which is white):
![lightmap_sunonly](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/21999379/103345349-13e9da80-4a89-11eb-9bee-d26ac5767f23.png)
Color is better, but because of the stochastic samples, a lot are hitting zero energy sky.

This also happens with PBR shading. I suspect the problem is two fold:
1) The balance between the energy of the direct sunlight and the diffuse from the blue sky is incorrect (probably that the sun contains way more energy than it appears)
2) Our eyes auto compensate for this white balance in shade from direct sunlight. This happens in real life but not in a photo.
See:
https://wtamu.edu/~cbaird/sq/2014/02/10/why-doesnt-the-outside-world-appear-blue-even-though-so-much-light-comes-from-the-blue-sky/

As the denoiser and embree are quite large libraries, I'd just like to confirm:

* They are not compiled in to non-tools builds
* They are easily compile-outable with an scons switch

This second point is so that devs who are working normally often end up having something cause a rebuild all, and it would be nice to be able to remove this functionality to decrease build time.

Overall though great work! :grinning: :+1:

Our buildsystem has SSE2 support and compiles binary for it, but for example on my Linux distro the i586 is without SSE2 so the generated binaries have greater compability (it's arguable whether using Embree without SSE2 on a Pentium III is really worth the pain, but well ;)).

Architecture wise, why is `LightmapRaycaster` part of `scene` when it seems designed only for use with Embree which is in `modules/raycast`? Should it all be in `modules/lightmapper` that would build all relevant dependencies and only make the `Lightmapper` node available when that module is built?

In other words, is there a use case for the modularity offered by having a generic structure in core, that is then enabled only by specific modules for each component?

To clarify, while most modules build a single thirdparty library, that's not a requirement. Modules are for content that can be enabled/disabled as needed, and if several libraries are necessary for either part to make sense as a whole, they can all be together.

I followed the same structure as LightmapDenoiser. Other than providing the possiblility of adding different raycast engines, this organization makes it easy to compile the editor when this module is disabled. AFAIK there is no real way to tell if a module is disabled outside the `modules` build environment, So there needs to be some common type in `scene` that may or may not be implemented by a module.
